title: Looking back: the Gurus' teachings
hookLine: Nanak's dialogues, the Gurus' voices, the Ninth's calm
tomorrow: Looking back: the Tenth Guru's pen

lines: A DIFFERENT GURU, THE SAME NAME.
cards: In a hymn by Guru Nanak, there's his name: Nanak. In a hymn by Guru Arjan, a later Guru, the same name appears: Nanak.
Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Tegh Bahadur: the Gurus whose hymns fill the Granth sign them as Nanak. To a newcomer, it can look like a mistake in the credits. To Sikhs, it's the point.
After the music, the voices: how different they sound, and why they're signed with one name.

teach.h: NANAK IN DIALOGUE: THE SIDH GOSHT.
teach.b: First, Nanak in dialogue. Guru Nanak doesn't only sing; he argues, gently. In the Sidh Gosht, yogis who have left the world question him: why stay among householders?
His answers keep returning to the Word, and to living truthfully in the world rather than fleeing it. Teaching, for him, could be a conversation. Second, how you tell the voices apart.
Each hymn carries a heading, Mahala one, Mahala two and so on, marking which Guru composed it, while the signature stays Nanak.
Listen across them: Guru Angad's spare sloks, Guru Amar Das's Anand, Guru Arjan's long Sukhmani. Different temperaments. One signature.
Third, the Ninth Guru's calm. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns have a stillness all their own.
In Raag Sorath he describes, in paraphrase, the person who isn't shaken by pain, isn't carried off by pleasure, holds praise and blame alike, and sees gold as dust.

It reads like the voice of someone who has already let go. Fourth, why one name. In the ballad of Balwand and Satta, they sing, in paraphrase, that the light was the same and the way was the same; only the body changed.
Sikhs understand the Gurus as one light passing from lamp to lamp. And around them, the bhagats, Kabir, Farid, Namdev and others, keep their own names, welcomed in.
Many voices, saying the truth in their own way, without needing to drown each other out.

how: Sikhs read and sing the hymns of the Gurus and the bhagats together in the Guru Granth Sahib; each hymn's heading names its raga and its Mahala, which tells readers which Guru composed it.

games.q: you're a yogi who has left the world behind, and you ask Guru Nanak why he still lives among householders. how does he answer?
o: he agrees to leave the world with you.
he points to the Word and to living truthfully in the world.
games.why: in the Sidh Gosht, his answers keep returning to the Word, lived in the world rather than fled from.

practice: Here are three teachings from three voices, in paraphrase. Guru Nanak: stay in the world, and live truthfully in it; Guru Arjan: all are sharers, and God is outside of no one; Guru Tegh Bahadur: hold praise and blame alike.
Let one of them choose you, and say it slowly, once on the in-breath, once on the out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. At the year's close, the Gurus' teachings: different voices, each hymn marked by its Mahala, all signed Nanak, one light passed on. Today's word.
